title: Fluids
note: Pressure is force per area, and in a fluid at rest it grows with depth as ρgh. A submerged object feels a buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid it displaces. In moving fluids, continuity (Av constant) and Bernoulli's equation link speed and pressure: where flow is faster, pressure is lower.

read.title: Pressure, buoyancy, and flow
text: A fluid pushes on every surface it touches. Pressure is that push per unit area, and at any point in a still fluid it acts equally in all directions. The deeper you go, the more fluid sits above you, so pressure increases by ρgh. In water that adds about one atmosphere every ten meters. The shape of the container does not matter; only depth, density, and the pressure at the surface do.

Because pressure grows with depth, the bottom of a submerged object is pushed up harder than its top is pushed down. The difference is the buoyant force, and Archimedes found its size: it equals the weight of the fluid the object displaces. A steel ship floats because its hull encloses so much air that its average density is less than water's.

Moving fluids obey two more rules. Continuity says an incompressible fluid must speed up where a pipe narrows, since the same volume passes each point per second. Bernoulli's equation is energy conservation for flowing fluid: where the speed rises, the pressure falls. Faster air over the curved top of a wing, at lower pressure than the air below, is part of how wings produce lift.
